draft.title: The first line of defence
card: The first line of defence is made of barriers that stop pathogens entering the body. It works against many kinds of pathogen and does not need to have met them before.

Intact skin is a tough, waterproof layer that most pathogens cannot pass. Mucous membranes line the airways and gut, and their sticky mucus traps microbes. Cilia are tiny hairs in the airways that sweep the mucus out.
Stomach acid kills many microbes that are swallowed. Tears contain an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of some bacteria, and they wash the eye.
These barriers stop most pathogens, but not all. A cut in the skin or a damaged lining gives pathogens a way in.
draft.remember: The first line of defence blocks, traps or kills pathogens before they get inside the body.

a.q: Which of these is a chemical barrier that helps stop pathogens entering the body?
opts: Stomach acid killing swallowed microbes
Cilia sweeping mucus out of the airways
Skin forming a waterproof layer
Mucus trapping microbes in the nose
a.why: Stomach acid is a chemical that kills microbes. Cilia, skin and mucus are physical barriers: they block, trap or sweep pathogens away rather than destroying them with a chemical.
a.clue: Look for the one that kills microbes with a chemical, not by blocking or trapping them.

b.q: Sam has a cold virus. He has a lot of mucus in his nose, and his cilia are moving it towards his throat. Which statement best describes what this shows?
opts: A barrier is trapping and removing pathogens
The body is making antibodies to the virus
Cells are engulfing the virus in inflamed tissue
The body is remembering a virus it met before
b.why: Mucus traps microbes and cilia sweep it away, which is part of the first line of defence. Antibodies are a different kind of response that targets one specific pathogen. Trapping and sweeping away does not need the body to have met the virus before.
b.clue: Mucus and cilia are barriers, so which option describes a barrier at work?

b.best: A barrier is trapping and removing pathogens

problems.detail: The clue says mucus and cilia are barriers and asks which option describes a barrier. Only one option contains the word 'barrier', so the clue gives the answer away.
Cilia are called 'tiny hairs'. They are hair-like projections on cells, not hairs, and students could confuse them with nose hairs. 'Tiny hair-like structures' would be accurate.

b.q: Sam has a cold virus. He has a lot of mucus in his nose, and his cilia are moving it towards his throat. Which statement best describes what this shows?
opts: Pathogens are being trapped and swept out of the airways
The body is making antibodies to the cold virus
Cells are engulfing the virus in inflamed tissue
The body is remembering a virus it met before
b.why: Mucus traps microbes and cilia sweep it away, which is the first line of defence acting before pathogens get inside. The antibody option is tempting, but mucus and cilia do not target one particular virus and do not need to have met it before.
b.clue: Where is the virus while the mucus and cilia act on it?
